name.text: C5.Q1 — Partial trace and reduced states

questiontext.text:
C5.Q1 — Marginals of a multipartite state

The partial trace is the unique operation reproducing all local measurement statistics. Implemented on the reshaped tensor it is a sequence of traces over paired axes.

Write partial_trace(rho, dims, keep) for a density matrix on subsystems of dimensions dims, keeping the (sorted) indices in keep; and purity(rho) returning \(\operatorname{tr}\rho^{2}\) as a float rounded to 6 decimals.

Bell state, keep=[0]  ->  I/2, purity 0.5
product state         ->  purity 1.0

testcode.text: import numpy as np bell = np.array([1,0,0,1], dtype=complex)/np.sqrt(2) rho = np.outer(bell, bell.conj()) print(np.round(partial_trace(rho, [2,2], [0]).real, 6).tolist())
import numpy as np bell = np.array([1,0,0,1], dtype=complex)/np.sqrt(2) rho = np.outer(bell, bell.conj()) print(purity(rho), purity(partial_trace(rho, [2,2], [0])))
import numpy as np v = np.zeros(4, dtype=complex); v[0]=1 rho = np.outer(v, v.conj()) print(purity(partial_trace(rho, [2,2], [1])))
import numpy as np ghz = np.zeros(8, dtype=complex); ghz[0]=ghz[7]=1/np.sqrt(2) rho = np.outer(ghz, ghz.conj()) r01 = partial_trace(rho, [2,2,2], [0,1]) print(r01.shape, purity(r01))

import numpy as np rng = np.random.default_rng(4) v = rng.normal(size=6) + 1j*rng.normal(size=6); v/=np.linalg.norm(v) rho = np.outer(v, v.conj()) rA = partial_trace(rho, [2,3], [0]) print(rA.shape, round(float(np.real(np.trace(rA))), 6))

name.text: C5.Q2 — Kraus operators and standard noise channels

questiontext.text:
C5.Q2 — Applying and validating a channel

A CPTP map has Kraus operators with \(\sum_k K_k^{\dagger}K_k=I\). Depolarizing, dephasing and amplitude damping are the workhorse noise models.

Write apply_kraus(rho, Ks); is_cptp(Ks, tol=1e-9) returning a bool; and the three constructors depolarizing(p), dephasing(p), amplitude_damping(g) returning lists of Kraus operators exactly as tabulated in §3.

depolarizing(1.0) applied to any rho  ->  I/2
amplitude_damping(1.0) applied to any rho  ->  |0><0|

testcode.text: import numpy as np print(is_cptp(depolarizing(0.3)), is_cptp(dephasing(0.2)), is_cptp(amplitude_damping(0.7)))
import numpy as np rho = np.array([[1,0],[0,0]], dtype=complex) print(np.round(apply_kraus(rho, depolarizing(1.0)).real, 6).tolist())
import numpy as np rho = np.array([[0,0],[0,1]], dtype=complex) print(np.round(apply_kraus(rho, amplitude_damping(1.0)).real, 6).tolist())
import numpy as np plus = np.array([1,1], dtype=complex)/np.sqrt(2) rho = np.outer(plus, plus.conj()) out = apply_kraus(rho, dephasing(0.5)) print(np.round(out.real, 6).tolist())

import numpy as np rng = np.random.default_rng(9) v = rng.normal(size=2)+1j*rng.normal(size=2); v/=np.linalg.norm(v) rho = np.outer(v, v.conj()) out = apply_kraus(rho, depolarizing(0.37)) print(round(float(np.real(np.trace(out))), 6))

name.text: C5.Q3 — The Choi matrix and complete positivity

questiontext.text:
C5.Q3 — Channel–state duality

The Choi–Jamiołkowski isomorphism turns a channel into a state: \(J(\mathcal E)=(\mathrm{id}\otimes\mathcal E)(|\Omega\rangle\langle\Omega|)\) with \(|\Omega\rangle=\tfrac1{\sqrt d}\sum_i|ii\rangle\). \(\mathcal E\) is completely positive iff \(J\ge0\).

Write choi(Ks, d=2) returning the \(d^{2}\times d^{2}\) Choi matrix of the channel with Kraus operators Ks; is_cp_from_choi(J, tol=1e-9) returning a bool (all eigenvalues \(\ge-\)tol); and kraus_rank(J, tol=1e-9) returning the number of strictly positive eigenvalues.

identity channel   ->  Choi = |Omega><Omega|, rank 1
depolarizing(1.0)  ->  rank 4

testcode.text: import numpy as np J = choi([np.eye(2, dtype=complex)]) print(np.round(J.real, 6).tolist())
import numpy as np J = choi([np.eye(2, dtype=complex)]) print(is_cp_from_choi(J), kraus_rank(J))

import numpy as np I2 = np.eye(2, dtype=complex) X = np.array([[0,1],[1,0]], dtype=complex) Y = np.array([[0,-1j],[1j,0]], dtype=complex) Z = np.array([[1,0],[0,-1]], dtype=complex) Ks = [np.sqrt(1-3*1.0/4)*I2, 0.5*X, 0.5*Y, 0.5*Z] J = choi(Ks) print(kraus_rank(J), np.allclose(J, np.eye(4)/4))

import numpy as np K0 = np.array([[1,0],[0,np.sqrt(1-0.3)]], dtype=complex) K1 = np.array([[0,np.sqrt(0.3)],[0,0]], dtype=complex) J = choi([K0, K1]) print(is_cp_from_choi(J), kraus_rank(J), round(float(np.real(np.trace(J))), 6))

import numpy as np # transposition is positive but not completely positive: its Choi matrix has a negative eigenvalue E = [np.array([[1,0],[0,0]], dtype=complex), np.array([[0,0],[0,1]], dtype=complex), np.array([[0,1],[0,0]], dtype=complex), np.array([[0,0],[1,0]], dtype=complex)] J = choi([np.eye(2, dtype=complex)]) Jt = J.reshape(2,2,2,2).transpose(0,3,2,1).reshape(4,4) print(is_cp_from_choi(Jt))

name.text: C5.Q4 — Trace distance, fidelity and data processing

questiontext.text:
C5.Q4 — How far apart are two states?

\(D=\tfrac12\|\rho-\sigma\|_1\) is the optimal distinguishing advantage; \(F\) is Uhlmann fidelity. Both are monotone under channels.

Write trace_distance(rho, sigma) and fidelity(rho, sigma) (\(F=(\operatorname{tr}\sqrt{\sqrt\rho\sigma\sqrt\rho})^{2}\)), each returning a float rounded to 6 decimals, and von_neumann(rho) returning \(S(\rho)\) in bits, rounded to 6 decimals, with eigenvalues clipped at 0 before taking logs.

D(|0>,|1>) = 1.0,   F(|0>,|1>) = 0.0
S(I/2) = 1.0,       S(|0><0|) = 0.0

testcode.text: import numpy as np r0 = np.array([[1,0],[0,0]], dtype=complex) r1 = np.array([[0,0],[0,1]], dtype=complex) print(trace_distance(r0,r1), fidelity(r0,r1))
import numpy as np I2 = np.eye(2, dtype=complex)/2 r0 = np.array([[1,0],[0,0]], dtype=complex) print(von_neumann(I2), von_neumann(r0))
import numpy as np r0 = np.array([[1,0],[0,0]], dtype=complex) plus = np.array([1,1], dtype=complex)/np.sqrt(2) rp = np.outer(plus, plus.conj()) print(trace_distance(r0,rp), fidelity(r0,rp))

import numpy as np I2 = np.eye(2, dtype=complex) X = np.array([[0,1],[1,0]], dtype=complex) Y = np.array([[0,-1j],[1j,0]], dtype=complex) Z = np.array([[1,0],[0,-1]], dtype=complex) p = 0.4 Ks = [np.sqrt(1-3*p/4)*I2, np.sqrt(p)/2*X, np.sqrt(p)/2*Y, np.sqrt(p)/2*Z] def ap(rho): return sum(K @ rho @ K.conj().T for K in Ks) r0 = np.array([[1,0],[0,0]], dtype=complex) r1 = np.array([[0,0],[0,1]], dtype=complex) print(trace_distance(ap(r0), ap(r1)) <= trace_distance(r0, r1))
import numpy as np rho = np.diag([0.7, 0.3]).astype(complex) print(von_neumann(rho))
